source.title_on_document: Your Brain on ChatGPT: Accumulation of Cognitive Debt when Using an AI Assistant for Essay Writing Task

supplement.where: Appendix A-BC is included on PDF pp. 167-216; the reading guide on p. 5 directs readers to it. No separate external statistical supplement is identified.
supplement.holds: Appendix A lists interview clusters; B-BC provide additional EEG visualizations and detailed dDTF tables, including connection sums, session patterns and significance markers. They do not supply arm SDs/SEs or treatment-effect tables for essay uniqueness or diversity.

paper_design_summary: Adults recruited from greater-Boston universities were randomly assigned to write SAT-prompt essays using ChatGPT, web search without LLMs, or no tools in supervised sessions; 54 people are analyzed, with 18 in each arm (pp. 22-28; Table 1, pp. 3-4). Essays were scored by blinded English teachers and an AI judge and compared using embeddings, named entities, n-grams and conceptual ontologies (pp. 52-84). An optional fourth session reused 18 participants from the original sample with tools switched; essays produced by former ChatGPT users in that session were unassisted (pp. 28, 45-46 and 117).

studies.label: Supervised essay-writing experiment with optional session-4 tool switch

assignment.what_was_assigned: Initial individual assignment to ChatGPT, Search Engine or Brain-only, balanced on age and gender, retained across the initial sessions (p. 23). Returning LLM and Brain-only participants switched tools in the optional later session; participation depended on availability and no separate random assignment at follow-up is reported (pp. 28, 45 and 117).
assignment.quote: Participants were randomly assigned across the three following groups, balanced with respect to age and gender:
assignment.locator: p. 23, Experimental Design: Participants; pp. 24 and 27-28, supervised protocol; p. 117, Session 4 clarification

arms.name: LLM Group (ChatGPT)
arms.description: ChatGPT was the only permitted information resource in sessions 1-3; a provided account was used, and other websites/LLMs were prohibited (pp. 23 and 27). Table 1 (p. 3) reports 18 analyzed per group. The original LLM returnee subgroup has 9 people and writes without tools in session 4 (pp. 28 and 46).

arms.name: Search Engine Group (web search; no LLM)
arms.description: Any website except LLMs; participants used Google, with "-ai" appended to queries to suppress AI-enhanced results (p. 23). Table 1 (pp. 3-4) reports 18 analyzed per group and no Search Engine session 4.

arms.name: Brain-only Group (no tools)
arms.description: No websites, online/offline tools or LLMs; participants relied on their own knowledge (pp. 23 and 27). Table 1 (p. 3) reports 18 analyzed per group. The original Brain-only returnee subgroup has 9 people and uses ChatGPT in session 4 (pp. 28, 46 and 117).

participants.exclusions: The methods report 60 recruited, 55 completing at least the initial three sessions, and data reported only for 54 "to ensure data distribution" (p. 22). Scheduling difficulties explain incomplete attendance; the omitted completed case, arm-specific losses, and numbers at randomization are not specified. Optional session 4 was completed by 18 members of this same sample (pp. 45-46, 117). Counts are analyzed, not randomized; no intention-to-treat analysis is claimed.
participants.who: Adults aged 18-39 recruited at MIT, Wellesley, Harvard, Tufts and Northeastern; predominantly undergraduate/postgraduate students, with university employees also described (p. 22). The education/occupation counts in the source are not fully consistent with the final analyzed total.
participants.country: United States (greater Boston, Massachusetts; pp. 1 and 22)
participants.quote: To ensure data distribution, we are here only reporting data from 54 participants (as participants were assigned in three groups, see details below).
participants.locator: p. 22, Experimental Design: Participants; p. 3, Table 1 (18 per group); pp. 45-46 and 117 (returning subset)

ai_tool.name_model: OpenAI ChatGPT; participant-facing model version not stated in the methods.
ai_tool.how_used: Participants used a supplied ChatGPT account as their only information resource and could prompt for drafting, ideas, organization, translation or editing; conversations were retained (pp. 23, 27 and 45). llama4:17b-scout-16e-instruct-q4_K_M was used by the researchers for NLP and AI judging (pp. 53, 58, 65, 68 and 72), not identified as the participant assistance model. ChatGPT was removed for LLM-to-Brain session-4 essays (p. 28).

task.description: Argumentative essays on SAT-style prompts: participants chose among 3 prompts in each of sessions 1-3, for 9 offered topics overall (p. 25). Session 4 offered each returnee only topics that person had previously written about (p. 28). These outputs qualify through rated uniqueness and across-writer similarity, not solely through general essay quality.
task.duration: 20 minutes per essay (p. 27). Initial three sessions plus an optional fourth; scheduling spanned four months, but individual intersession delays are not stated (pp. 23 and 28).

outcomes.name: Essay uniqueness rated by English teachers
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Two English teachers, blinded to assignment and even the existence of the study groups, scored essays from 0 (not at all) to 5 (excellent), p. 72. Essay-score distributions and averages are shown by group, topic and session, rather than a participant-level treatment-effect model. Raw-score, z-score and topic-specific displays are variants of the same outcome; z-scores are not between-arm standardized effects. This entry covers writing with ChatGPT available in the assisted condition; pooled displays do not consistently isolate sessions 1-3 from session 4.

contrasts.reported: Teachers describe lower uniqueness for essays they perceived as AI-written, while noting exceptions with unique examples or quotations. Topic-specific patterns vary: HAPPINESS and LOYALTY discussions describe low teacher uniqueness for LLM essays, whereas ART uniqueness is described as high. No exact LLM-versus-Brain-only arm contrast, SD, SE or confidence interval is printed.
contrasts.locator: p. 72, AI judge vs Human teachers; pp. 73-76, Figs. 41 and 44-47; pp. 80-82, Figs. 52-53

contrasts.control_arm: Search Engine Group (web search; no LLM)
contrasts.reported: Teacher uniqueness is displayed by tool group and topic, but the text does not give an exact LLM-versus-Search Engine contrast or inferential test. This code denotes insufficient comparative evidence, not a demonstrated null effect.
contrasts.locator: pp. 72-76, AI judge vs Human teachers, Fig. 41; pp. 76-84, Figs. 47-55

outcomes.name: Within-group semantic similarity of essays
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Embeddings generated using llama4:17b-scout-16e-instruct-q4_K_M; pairwise cosine similarity/distance among essays in each tool group, displayed as heatmaps (p. 57, Fig. 19). PaCMAP topic/group clustering in Figures 13-14 is a related descriptive visualization. This outcome concerns different writers; the same-writer session-change analysis is recorded separately.

contrasts.reported: The text describes greater similarity in LLM essays and Figure 19 shows within-group pairwise heatmaps. No numeric arm-average similarity, SD, SE, confidence interval or comparison p-value is printed. Lower diversity is coded, reversing the reported similarity direction.
contrasts.locator: pp. 53-54, Figs. 13-14; p. 57, Fig. 19 and preceding paragraph; p. 143, Discussion: NLP

contrasts.control_arm: Search Engine Group (web search; no LLM)
contrasts.reported: The authors describe LLM essays as more homogeneous and less variable than the other groups; no exact LLM-versus-Search Engine similarity contrast or uncertainty is printed. Direction follows the authors' description, not a calculated difference between heatmap colors.
contrasts.locator: p. 57, Fig. 19; p. 143, Discussion: NLP

diversity_detail.metric: Pairwise cosine similarity between essay embeddings; greater similarity means lower diversity.
diversity_detail.computed_over: All essay pairs within each tool group, according to Fig. 19. Repeated essays per writer occur in the study; exclusion of within-writer pairs and separation by session are not stated for this heatmap.
diversity_detail.uncertainty: No participant-clustered SE, bootstrap/permutation procedure, numeric comparative test or confidence interval is specified for this outcome.
diversity_detail.notes: Similarity direction is reversed. No arm-level effect estimate or count of analyzed pairs is supplied.

outcomes.name: Consistency of named-entity distributions (Cramer's V)
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Named entities were extracted and classified using llama4:17b-scout-16e-instruct-q4_K_M. Entity-frequency contingency tables were summarized using Cramer's V and averaged across topics (pp. 58-59). Figure 21 contains comparison p-values inside the raster figure, absent from the markdown. Bars have no numeric value labels, so heights are not transcribed as exact Cramer's V estimates.

contrasts.reported: Cramer's V is higher for LLM than Brain Only; the comparison bracket is labeled "* 0.02898". Exact arm Cramer's V values and SEs are not printed. Greater consistency is coded as lower diversity.
contrasts.locator: pp. 58-59, Named Entities Recognition; p. 59, Fig. 21

contrasts.control_arm: Search Engine Group (web search; no LLM)
contrasts.reported: Cramer's V is higher for LLM than Search Engine; the comparison bracket is labeled "** 0.00462". Exact arm Cramer's V values and SEs are not printed. Greater consistency is coded as lower diversity.
contrasts.locator: pp. 58-59, Named Entities Recognition; p. 59, Fig. 21

diversity_detail.metric: Cramer's V for association/consistency in named-entity distributions, averaged by topic.
diversity_detail.embedding_model: Not an embedding measure; entity classification uses llama4:17b-scout-16e-instruct-q4_K_M.
diversity_detail.computed_over: Named-entity frequencies from essays within each tool group and topic, subsequently averaged across topics; contingency-table layout and effective independent sample size are not fully specified.
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Fig. 21 prints pairwise comparison p-values but does not identify the test, sampling unit or handling of repeated essays/participants. No SE or confidence interval is supplied.
diversity_detail.notes: The paper interprets larger V as greater consistency; the atlas direction is reversed. Entity frequencies and V are not counts of people.

outcomes.name: Repetition and overlap of n-grams across essays
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Frequencies and overlaps of lemmatized n-grams of lengths 2-5 are displayed across topics/tool groups (pp. 62-65, Figs. 25-27). Session/topic breakdowns using n-grams occurring at least 3 times per essay appear in pp. 132-136, Figs. 79-86. The latter text also describes Figure 27 as using order 4 and higher, an unresolved difference in definitions. Topic/session displays are variants; post-AI production is separated below.

contrasts.reported: The authors describe LLM essays as more repetitive and Brain-only essays as more variable. For CHOICES, the text says LLM and Search Engine essays remained repetitive while Brain-only essays had a highly diverse range. No overall overlap coefficient, arm SD, SE or comparative test is reported.
contrasts.locator: pp. 62-65, Figs. 25-27; p. 133, Fig. 81 and text; p. 143, Discussion: NLP

contrasts.control_arm: Search Engine Group (web search; no LLM)
contrasts.reported: The groups have different topic-specific lexical patterns; both LLM and Search Engine show repeated phrases. No single numerical LLM-versus-Search Engine diversity contrast is reported.

diversity_detail.metric: Frequency and overlap of repeated lemmatized n-grams.
diversity_detail.computed_over: Essay pools within tool group and topic, with pooled and session-specific displays; not a within-person idea-category count.
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Descriptive bubble/frequency and flow diagrams; no specified sampling procedure, SE or overall inferential comparison.
diversity_detail.notes: Greater repetition corresponds to lower diversity. The paper gives examples and distributions rather than an arm-level diversity score.

outcomes.name: Between-group divergence of n-gram distributions (KL divergence)
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Kullback-Leibler divergence between aggregated group n-gram distributions, normalized within topic, with smoothing epsilon = 1e-10; the top-left heatmap aggregates across topics (pp. 57-58, Fig. 20). This measures how group distributions differ from one another and cannot by itself rank diversity within each group.

contrasts.reported: The text reports Brain-only divergence from LLM for ART, CHOICES, COURAGE, FORETHOUGHT and PHILANTHROPY; LOYALTY and HAPPINESS show less difference between LLM and Brain-only. No numeric KL cell labels, exact arm-level contrast or uncertainty are printed. Topic-specific distribution separation is not a signed within-group diversity effect.
contrasts.locator: pp. 57-58, Similarities and distances; p. 58, Fig. 20

contrasts.control_arm: Search Engine Group (web search; no LLM)
contrasts.reported: The text reports the Search Engine distribution diverging most in LOYALTY and HAPPINESS, with other patterns in other topics. The heatmaps do not establish which of these two groups has greater internal diversity.
contrasts.locator: pp. 57-58, Similarities and distances; p. 58, Fig. 20

diversity_detail.metric: Kullback-Leibler divergence between group-level n-gram frequency distributions.
diversity_detail.computed_over: Aggregated n-gram distributions for pairs of tool groups, separately by topic and in an all-topic summary; not individual essay-pair distances.
diversity_detail.uncertainty: No test method, numeric comparison p-value, SE or confidence interval is supplied for Fig. 20.
diversity_detail.notes: Direction is mixed because distribution separation does not identify a higher-diversity treatment arm. Normalized heatmap colors are not precise numerical estimates.

outcomes.name: Shared conceptual relationships in essay ontologies
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Essay ontology graphs were generated with llama4:17b-scout-16e-instruct-q4_K_M and manually checked (p. 68). The analysis counts recurring edges across different essays on the same topic within each group, matching node wording using Levenshtein distance <= 10 (p. 70, Fig. 37). The topic-level variant uses <= 20 (p. 71, Fig. 38).

contrasts.reported: The authors report that LLM essays dominate repeated ontology edges, while Brain-only essays have only a handful of frequent edges and little intersection with the other tool groups. No overall overlap estimate, SD, SE or numeric inferential comparison is reported.
contrasts.locator: pp. 68-71, Ontology analysis, Figs. 34 and 37-38; p. 145, Discussion: NLP

contrasts.control_arm: Search Engine Group (web search; no LLM)
contrasts.reported: Search Engine essays are described as largely overlapping with LLM essays in reused ontology, but no clear scalar comparison of their internal diversity is given. No numeric treatment contrast or uncertainty is printed.
contrasts.locator: p. 70, Fig. 37 and text; p. 145, Discussion: NLP

diversity_detail.metric: Counts of ontology edges recurring across essays after approximate matching of node labels.
diversity_detail.embedding_model: Not an embedding similarity measure; ontology extraction uses llama4:17b-scout-16e-instruct-q4_K_M.
diversity_detail.computed_over: Edges from each essay compared with other essays on the same topic within the same tool group; further aggregated across groups/topics.
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Descriptive graph/count visualizations; no specified participant-level SE, confidence interval or quantitative comparative test.
diversity_detail.notes: More recurring relationships imply less conceptual diversity. Graph matching thresholds are tuning choices, not effect estimates.

outcomes.name: Uniqueness of unassisted essays after prior ChatGPT use
outcomes.question: after_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: The same blinded teacher uniqueness rubric is applied to session-4 essays produced by LLM-to-Brain returnees after ChatGPT was removed (pp. 28, 72 and 117). This is the returning subset, not a new independent sample. Figures 47-55 show session-4 points among earlier-session scores. The text does not supply a dedicated controlled after-AI uniqueness effect; comparisons across current tool groups/sessions must not be read as a randomized retention estimate.
outcomes.delay: Session 4 after the earlier assisted sessions; elapsed days are not stated. The four-month period on p. 23 describes study scheduling, not an individual follow-up interval.

contrasts.reported: The session-4 discussion describes low uniqueness on FORETHOUGHT and PERFECT for LLM-to-Brain essays. Elsewhere the paper states that session-4 essays were generally scored highly. No exact after-AI versus earlier Brain-only mean difference, SD, SE, confidence interval or comparison p-value is printed. This is a nonconcurrent descriptive comparison.
contrasts.locator: p. 76, Scoring per topic; pp. 80 and 83, Figs. 51 and 54; p. 122, Cognitive processing

contrasts.reported: The summary describes session-4 LLM-to-Brain essays as scoring higher by teachers within the group, while topic-specific discussion highlights low uniqueness. No uniqueness-specific before/after effect or uncertainty is printed.
contrasts.locator: pp. 3-4, Table 1; p. 76, Scoring per topic; p. 122, Cognitive processing

outcomes.question: after_ai

The same n-gram analysis as the assisted outcome is separated here because the scored essays were produced after AI removal. The discussion interprets repeated phrasing as a narrower set of ideas but provides no single participant-level diversity score.
outcomes.delay: Session 4 after the earlier assisted sessions; elapsed days are not stated. The four-month period on p. 23 describes study scheduling, not an individual follow-up interval.

COURAGE, FORETHOUGHT and PERFECT are highlighted as examples of a narrower set of ideas. No numerical diversity contrast or uncertainty is printed, and the authors call this finding preliminary.
contrasts.locator: pp. 133-136, Figs. 81-86 and summary; p. 151, Session 4 discussion

contrasts.control_arm: LLM Group, earlier assisted essays on the same topics
contrasts.reported: LLM-to-Brain essays reused previously common LLM wording in FORETHOUGHT and PERFECT. The text reports persistence of phrases rather than a numerical increase or decrease in diversity relative to prior assisted writing.
contrasts.locator: pp. 134-136, Figs. 83 and 85 and summary

diversity_detail.metric: Repeated n-grams and descriptive overlap of topic-specific vocabularies.
diversity_detail.computed_over: Session-4 unassisted essays from former LLM users, summarized by topic and compared with earlier LLM and Brain-only essay pools. Graphs mix group-level overlap with reuse across sessions.
diversity_detail.uncertainty: No SE, confidence interval or quantitative comparison test. The authors explicitly call for a larger sample (pp. 136 and 151).
diversity_detail.notes: Lower diversity is the authors' interpretation of narrower/repeated phrasing. This selected returning subset has no concurrent never-AI unassisted control; it is not an independent core study.

outcomes.name: Change in the same writer's essay after ChatGPT removal (PaCMAP distance)
outcomes.question: after_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Normalized PaCMAP distances between a participant's session-4 essay and an earlier essay on the same topic, averaged per participant/topic (pp. 52-53, Fig. 12); embedding model identified in Figs. 13-14 as llama4:17b-scout-16e-instruct-q4_K_M. This measures within-writer change, not diversity across people, and does not directly measure improvement in creativity. Only the LLM-to-Brain transition is coded here. Figure 12 also displays Search Engine transitions unexplained by the stated session-4 protocol.
outcomes.delay: Session 4 after the earlier assisted sessions; elapsed days are not stated. The four-month period on p. 23 describes study scheduling, not an individual follow-up interval.

contrasts.control_arm: The same returnees' earlier ChatGPT-assisted essay on the matched topic
contrasts.reported: The authors describe a significant distance after switching to Brain-only; Figure 12 shows normalized distances without numeric bar labels, test statistics, p-values or uncertainty. A larger distance is change in content/structure, not necessarily greater creativity. The unexplained Search Engine transitions prevent treating the full figure as a clean implementation of the stated crossover.
contrasts.locator: pp. 52-53, Fig. 12 and caption; pp. 23 and 28, session protocol; p. 117, Session 4 sample clarification

sample_overlap.shares_participants_with: No other paper is identified as the source of these participants. Within this paper, session 4 reuses the original experiment's participants and is not an independent sample.
sample_overlap.quote: we only present results for these 18 participants who took part in all 4 sessions.
sample_overlap.locator: p. 117, Session 4 sample clarification; pp. 22-23, original recruitment

company_involvement.description: The conflict statement reports that Nataliya Kosmyna held a Visiting Researcher position at Google at publication, while stating that all project work was completed before that affiliation. The remaining authors report no conflicts. The funding statement says there was no external funding.
company_involvement.locator: p. 154, Conflict of Interest and Funding

eligibility.reason: Initial individual random assignment to ChatGPT, non-AI web search, or no tools is explicit (p. 23), and the supervised protocol supports lab_rct (pp. 24, 27-28). The main study analyzes 54 people across all arms, with 18 in each (p. 22; Table 1, p. 3). Teacher-rated essay uniqueness and computed across-writer similarity are scored on produced output (p. 72; pp. 57-59, Figs. 19-21), satisfying the creative-writing/diversity scope even though the paper emphasizes EEG and learning. Eligibility rests on the initial experiment, not the optional 18-person follow-up. Usable participant-level precision for pooling is not supplied for the retained creative outcomes.

one_line_finding: Among 54 analyzed participants (p. 22), ChatGPT-assisted essays had greater named-entity consistency than Brain-only essays (p = 0.02898) and Search Engine essays (p = 0.00462), indicating lower diversity under the paper's interpretation (p. 59, Fig. 21).
open_questions: What is the exact revision date/arXiv version of the saved PDF? Its publication prose says June 2025 (pp. 151, 154), but reference 129 was retrieved December 12, 2025 (p. 166).
How many people were randomized, and when/why were participants omitted by arm? The methods give recruited/completer/analyzed totals, not an assignment flow (p. 22).

Can the underlying essay scores and NLP outputs provide arm means, participant-level SDs and uncertainty accounting for repeated essays? The PDF does not identify a data/code repository; p. 5 gives only https://www.brainonllm.com/.

What statistical test and independent sampling unit produced the Fig. 21 p-values, and what are the exact Cramer's V values? The contingency-table setup and uncertainty procedure are incomplete (pp. 58-59).
Which essays/sessions contribute to each pooled NLP and scoring display, and are within-writer pairs excluded from the within-group similarity heatmaps (pp. 52-59 and 73-76)?
Why does Fig. 12 include Search Engine transitions when Table 1 says there was no Search Engine session 4 and the protocol describes only LLM/Brain switches (pp. 4, 28, 52-53, 117)?

What does the word-variability p-value plot test? Its stated significant variability conclusion is not supported by an identified between-group test, and the prose alternates between word length and number of words (p. 55, Fig. 15).

Session-4 labels need reconciliation: the quoting-results section assigns poor performance to the reassigned LLM group, whereas the discussion attributes it to LLM-to-Brain (pp. 46-47 versus p. 150). Those recall results are not coded as creativity outcomes.
notes: Screened independently as A on 2026-10-09. Read the complete markdown, including all appendices, and checked relevant design/count/result passages against PDF page text. PDF page numbers equal printed page numbers; the actual Appendix begins on p. 167. Inspected raster figures directly in memory to verify the printed Fig. 21 p-values and Fig. 16 means; no plot-height estimates or derived effect sizes were recorded. One study is recorded because the main results and optional tool switch use the same experiment/sample. The procedural pilot on p. 23 reports no creative-output results and is not a separate screened dataset. The form's 15-outcome cap is applied. Omitted from separate entries: word-count/word-length dispersion (p. 55, Fig. 15); cosine distance to a model-generated reference essay (pp. 55-56, Figs. 17-18, reference distance rather than across-person diversity); raw named-entity frequency profiles (pp. 60-62, Figs. 22-24); teacher/AI language-and-style or vocabulary, grammar/accuracy, and rubric length ratings; and remaining session-4 rubric outcomes (pp. 72-84). Topic, session, raw-score and z-score variants are consolidated where they measure the same construct. EEG, quoting/recall, perceived ownership, satisfaction, prompt-use classifications, AI-authorship detection and energy estimates are not creative-output outcomes for the atlas and are excluded. No preregistered or explicitly designated primary creative outcome was found. Session-4 after-AI entries refer only to essays written by LLM-to-Brain returnees without tools. Brain-to-LLM essays still have AI available. The returning sample is selected by availability and has no concurrent never-AI unassisted control; cross-session/current-tool comparisons do not isolate a clean causal after-AI effect. Teacher versus AI-judge score disagreements are assessor differences, not treatment effects. Similarity/consistency signs are reversed for diversity, but between-group KL separation and same-writer PaCMAP change cannot establish a higher-diversity or higher-creativity arm. Fig. 16 word means do not support the blanket summary claim that Brain-only essays were shortest (Table 1, p. 4); both length variants are preserved as printed.
